subject: English
chapter: Hornbill (Prose): The Portrait of a Lady
text: The Portrait of a Lady by Khushwant Singh is a moving prose memoir about the author's grandmother and their evolving relationship over three phases. In the village, she was his caretaker — waking him, feeding him, walking him to the temple school, and feeding chapattis to the village dogs. In the city, their bond weakened: he went to an English school by bus, learnt science and Western ideas she disapproved of, and she turned to feeding sparrows. In old age, when he returned from abroad, she celebrated with drums and singing, overexerted herself, fell ill and died peacefully. At her death, thousands of sparrows gathered silently and flew away without eating the bread — a moving tribute. Themes: love and companionship across generations, the impact of modern education on tradition, and the quiet strength and spirituality of the grandmother.

subject: English
chapter: Hornbill (Prose): We're Not Afraid to Die if We Can All Be Together
text: This account by Gordon Cook and Alan East narrates a family's terrifying sea voyage. The narrator, his wife Mary, and children Jonathan (6) and Suzanne (7) set out to sail around the world on their boat Wavewalker. In the southern Indian Ocean they meet a gigantic wave that badly damages the boat and injures the narrator. Through immense courage, teamwork and determination, they pump out water, make repairs, and navigate to the tiny Ile Amsterdam island. The children's bravery stands out — Jonathan's line 'We're not afraid to die if we can all be together' gives the title. Themes: courage in the face of danger, family unity, optimism, hope, and human endurance against nature.

subject: English
chapter: Hornbill (Prose): Discovering Tut: the Saga Continues
text: Discovering Tut by A.R. Williams describes the study of the mummy of the boy-king Tutankhamun, the last ruler of a powerful dynasty of ancient Egypt, who died mysteriously as a teenager. In 1922 Howard Carter discovered his tomb full of treasures. The text explains how, in 2005, the mummy was taken out and put through a CT scan to investigate the cause of his death, revealing new details. It also recounts the damage done to the mummy by early explorers seeking gold. Themes: the intersection of archaeology, science and history; the mysteries of the past; and modern technology (CT scanning) revealing secrets of ancient civilisations.

subject: English
text: The Adventure by Jayant Narlikar is a science-fiction story blending history with quantum physics. Professor Gangadharpant Gaitonde, a historian, has an accident and finds himself in an alternate reality where history took a different course — the Marathas won the Battle of Panipat (1761), so India was never fully colonised by the British and developed differently. He experiences this parallel world, then returns to his own. The physicist Rajendra Deshpande later explains it using the theory of catastrophe and quantum concepts (many-worlds interpretation) — reality can branch into different possibilities. Themes: alternate history, the science of parallel universes, determinism versus possibility, and the imaginative link between history and physics.

subject: English
text: Silk Road by Nick Middleton is a travelogue describing the author's difficult journey to Mount Kailash for the sacred Kora (pilgrimage). Travelling across the Tibetan plateau, he crosses high mountain passes, meets shepherds and locals, sees wildlife, and endures harsh cold, altitude sickness and rough terrain. His companions Tsetan (the driver) and others help him along the way. On reaching Darchen (near Kailash), he falls ill with a cold and altitude problems, is treated by a Tibetan doctor, and recovers. The narrative is rich with descriptions of the landscape and people. Themes: the spirit of adventure and pilgrimage, human endurance, cultural encounter, and the beauty and hardship of remote regions.

subject: English
text: A Photograph by Shirley Toulson is a poem about memory, loss and the passage of time, across three layered moments. First, an old photograph shows the poet's mother as a young girl of about twelve, with two cousins (Betty and Dolly), at the beach, their feet paddling in the sea — the sea has not changed but the girls have. Second, the poet recalls her mother, years later, laughing fondly at that photograph and her 'sweet face'. Third, the poet mourns her mother's death, now silent in her own memory. The 'terribly transient feet' show how everything human is temporary while nature endures. Themes: transience of human life versus the permanence of nature, memory, and grief over a mother's loss. Devices: transferred epithet, imagery.

subject: English
text: The Laburnum Top by Ted Hughes vividly describes a still, silent laburnum tree in a September afternoon, its leaves yellowing and seeds fallen. The stillness is broken by the arrival of a goldfinch bird, which flits to the tree with a 'twitching chirrup' to feed her young hidden inside. Her movements make the whole tree tremble and come alive with sound and motion. After feeding, she flies away, and the tree returns to silence and stillness. The tree and the bird are shown as interdependent — the bird's presence gives the tree life. Themes: the interdependence of nature, the contrast between stillness and activity, and life and energy in the natural world. Devices: simile, metaphor, onomatopoeia, imagery.

subject: English
chapter: Hornbill (Poetry): The Voice of the Rain
text: The Voice of the Rain by Walt Whitman is a conversation between the poet and the rain. The poet asks the rain who it is, and the rain answers that it is the 'Poem of Earth'. It describes its eternal water cycle: it rises intangibly from the land and sea, forms clouds in the sky, changes shape, and falls back to wash the droughts and dust, giving life to seeds, and then returns again — an endless cycle. The rain compares itself to a poem/song that originates from its source (the poet's heart), goes out into the world, and eventually returns with love. Themes: the water cycle and the giving nature of rain, the cyclical unity of nature, and the parallel between rain and poetry (both give and return). Devices: personification, metaphor, imagery.

subject: English
text: Childhood by Markus Natten explores when and how one loses childhood and gains adult understanding. The poet keeps asking, 'When did my childhood go?' He suggests several possibilities: perhaps when he turned eleven and realised that Hell and Heaven could not be found in Geography; or when he saw that adults were hypocrites — preaching love but not practising it; or when he understood that his mind was truly his own, capable of independent thought. He concludes that his lost childhood has gone to a forgotten place — hidden in an infant's innocent face. Themes: loss of innocence, the transition from childhood to adulthood, rational thinking, and adult hypocrisy. Devices: rhetorical questions, imagery.

subject: English
text: Father to Son by Elizabeth Jennings expresses the pain of a strained relationship between a father and his grown son. The father laments that although he has lived with his son for years and they share the same home, he does not understand him — they have grown like strangers. He longs for the closeness they once had and does not know how to reach out. The son too seems distant and silent. Both are sorrowful; the father is willing to forgive and reconcile, extending 'empty hands', yet the gap remains. Themes: the generation gap, lack of communication, alienation within a family, and the sorrow and longing for reconciliation. Devices: imagery, symbolism ('empty hands'), tone of regret.

subject: English
chapter: Snapshots: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse
text: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse by William Saroyan is set in an Armenian community famous for honesty and trust. Two poor cousins, Aram and Mourad, belong to the Garoghlanian tribe. One morning Mourad turns up with a beautiful white horse, which he has actually taken (stolen) from a farmer, John Byro. The boys, who love riding, keep the horse hidden and ride it, though Aram is troubled by the family's reputation for honesty. When John Byro recognises his horse but, trusting the tribe's honesty, does not accuse them, the boys quietly return the horse. Themes: the innocence and desires of childhood, the conflict between temptation and moral values, and the family's proud tradition of honesty and trust. Devices: humour, characterisation.

subject: English
text: The Address by Marga Minco is a poignant post-World War II story about loss and broken connections. The narrator, whose mother died in the war, revisits an address — Number 46, Marconi Street — where her mother's belongings had been given for safekeeping to a Mrs Dorling during the war. On her first visit, Mrs Dorling coldly refuses to recognise her. On a second visit, the narrator is let in by Mrs Dorling's daughter and sees all her mother's familiar possessions being carelessly used in a strange, tasteless setting. Surrounded by these objects that now feel meaningless without her mother, she decides to leave them behind and forget the address. Themes: the horrors and aftermath of war, loss, human greed and heartlessness, and how objects lose meaning when detached from loved ones.

subject: English
text: Mother's Day by J.B. Priestley is a humorous one-act play with a social message about the unappreciated housewife. Mrs Annie Pearson is a devoted mother taken for granted by her husband George and children Doris and Cyril, who order her about and never help. Her confident neighbour Mrs Fitzgerald offers to teach the family a lesson by magically swapping their personalities (bodies) for a while. In Mrs Pearson's body, Mrs Fitzgerald behaves boldly — smoking, drinking stout, refusing to serve them and speaking bluntly — which shocks the family into realising how badly they have treated their mother. The personalities are switched back, and the family resolves to treat Mrs Pearson with respect. Themes: respect and appreciation for the homemaker, family responsibility, and gender roles, told with humour.

subject: English
text: Birth by A.J. Cronin portrays the dedication of a young doctor. Andrew Manson, a newly qualified doctor in a Welsh mining town, is called late at night to attend a difficult childbirth for Susan Morgan. After a long struggle, the baby is born but appears stillborn — lifeless and not breathing — while the mother is also in critical condition. Torn between saving mother and child, Andrew works desperately; through his skill and perseverance (alternating hot and cold water and resuscitation), he revives the seemingly dead baby, which finally cries and breathes. Exhausted but joyful, he feels he has done 'something real'. Themes: the nobility and dedication of the medical profession, perseverance, the miracle of life, and professional commitment. Devices: suspense, vivid description.

subject: English
chapter: Snapshots: The Tale of Melon City
text: The Tale of Melon City by Vikram Seth is a humorous narrative poem satirising governance. A 'just and placid' king orders an arch built across the road; when he rides through, the low arch knocks off his crown. Enraged, he decides to hang the chief builder, who blames the workmen, who blame the masons, who blame the architect, who reminds the king that he himself had altered the plans. To decide, the king consults the wisest man, who says the arch (a lifeless thing) should be punished — but then the arch is spared because it touched the royal head. Finally, a noose is set up, and the only person tall enough to fit it is the king himself, who is thus hanged. The people then let a passing idiot choose the next king, who picks a melon — so a melon 'rules' the city. Themes: satire on foolish, unjust and arbitrary rule, and the absurdity of a leadership that values custom over sense. Devices: irony, humour, absurdity.

subject: English
text: Tenses show the time of an action. Present: simple (writes), continuous (is writing), perfect (has written), perfect continuous (has been writing). Past: simple (wrote), continuous (was writing), perfect (had written), perfect continuous (had been writing). Future: simple (will write), continuous, perfect. Correct tense is chosen by context, sequence, and time markers; gap-filling tests this. Clauses are groups of words with a subject and verb. Main (independent) clause makes complete sense alone. Subordinate (dependent) clauses do not and are of three types: (1) Noun clause (acts as a noun, e.g. 'I know that he is honest'), (2) Adjective/Relative clause (describes a noun, begins with who/which/that, e.g. 'The book that I read'), (3) Adverb clause (modifies the verb; shows time, cause, condition, etc., e.g. 'because it rained').

subject: English
text: Gap filling tests correct use of grammar in context — filling blanks with the right tense, article (a/an/the), preposition, determiner, modal, or connector so the passage reads correctly. Read the whole sentence for clues (time words, subject-verb agreement) before choosing. Editing/omission tasks require finding an incorrect word and giving the correction. Sentence re-ordering (jumbled sentences): rearrange given words/phrases into a grammatically correct and meaningful sentence. Method: locate the subject and main verb, keep articles/adjectives with their nouns, place phrases logically, and ensure the sentence makes complete sense. These tasks assess accuracy in grammar, syntax and sentence structure.

subject: English
chapter: Writing Skills: Classified Advertisements and Posters
text: Classified advertisements are short notices grouped under categories (Situation Vacant, To Let, For Sale, Lost and Found, Matrimonial). They are brief, factual and boxed, using a telegraphic style and abbreviations to save space; include the category, essential details (item, condition, price, contact) in about 50 words. Posters are visual appeals to create awareness of an event or cause. A good poster has a catchy title/slogan, the main issue/purpose, essential details (date, time, venue), the issuing authority/organisation, and often a call to action, presented in an attractive but clear layout. Marks are awarded for format, content (relevant details) and creativity/expression.

subject: English
chapter: Writing Skills: Speech and Debate Writing
text: A speech is written to be spoken before an audience. Format: begin with a salutation and greeting (Respected Principal, teachers and my dear friends), introduce the topic, then the body with clear points, examples and persuasion, and end with a strong concluding appeal and a thank you. Use direct address, rhetorical questions and an engaging tone. A debate presents a strong argument for OR against a motion. Format: salutation, state your stand (for/against the motion), then present logical arguments with facts, evidence and examples, counter the opposing view, and close with a firm conclusion. Both require a formal, persuasive style, coherent structure, and appropriate connectors. Marks are for format, content (relevant, convincing points), expression and fluency.
